## TL;DR

This session addressed the latest review’s handoff drift and board-root lookup findings. Handoff’s final local check now acquires a check-gate lock, and its HEAD drift comparison uses the shared bookkeeping-path policy: `work/**` and `.repoos/**` changes are tolerated; other paths fail closed and include commit subjects and paths in the explanation. Deferred commit flushing no longer restores captured file snapshots over the current file contents. The server’s commit hook now consistently uses its configured board root.

The required `REPOOS_CHECK_CHANGED=main repoos check` passed after correcting a root-resolution regression discovered by the first run. The first remote run failed two existing check-gate tests because a process-wide environment value retained a previous test’s temporary root. The focused gate suite then passed all 14 tests, and the subsequent required scoped check passed its remote build and scoped tests, local guards, UI smoke, and rendered contrast audit.

This does not yet close every issue in review pass 4. The lock lifecycle remains wired only around the handoff local check; the managed self-check and close-out paths still need lifecycle coverage. The queue still needs cross-process read-modify-write serialization and a race-safe release/recovery protocol. The generic source-write helper is tested but is not yet the common production write path for all engineer filesystem writes. I am leaving these gaps explicit rather than describing the full acceptance criteria as met.

## Work and rationale

The previous handoff implementation decided that HEAD movement was harmless only when every changed path was the current task’s own task Markdown file. That missed review notes, report records, and other files below `work/`, even though those paths are bookkeeping. I replaced this special case with `checkGateHeadDriftAllowed`, which already owns the intended path classification and fails closed when Git cannot produce a diff. The helper also formats the offending commit subject and its source paths, allowing the handoff refusal to distinguish a bookkeeping commit from a real source edit.

I wired `acquireCheckGateLock` into the handoff’s actual `runCheck` path. It reads the checked-out branch, binds the lock to the server’s board root and the task’s worktree, reports acquisition failures as check failures, and releases the lock in `finally` so ordinary pass, fail, and cancellation returns do not leave it held. This is deliberately scoped to the local handoff check; the remote pre-review and other gate entry points still require review and lifecycle wiring.

I also corrected `commitFiles` to resolve its lock store from `REPOOS_BOARD_ROOT` before the check-store fallback or the commit root. `installCheckGateCommitHook` installs the active config’s board root. Without that, a commit issued from a task worktree could look for a lock under that worktree instead of the server’s board checkout and silently bypass the deferral hook.

The deferred queue recorded content snapshots and replayed them by rewriting files before commit. That made an old snapshot capable of replacing newer bookkeeping edits, and the empty-string sentinel could not distinguish an empty file from a deleted file. Flush now commits the current on-disk state for the queued paths and lets Git’s path-scoped add observe deletions. The queue entry remains present if commit fails. This removes destructive snapshot restoration, but it does not yet solve concurrent writers or serialize queue mutations across processes.

Documentation already describes bookkeeping tolerance, source commit refusals, and stale-lock cleanup in `user-docs/check.md`, with a corresponding workflow pointer in `docs/agent-workflow-rules.md`; I did not broaden those claims in this session.

## Approaches tried

I first ran the required scoped check after making the handoff and queue changes. Its remote validation built successfully but reported two failures in the check-gate bookkeeping tests: bookkeeping commits were not being deferred in two test setups. Running the focused test file reproduced the failures locally. Inspection showed that the hook’s board-root environment value was initialized only once and leaked from an earlier temporary repository into later test cases. Updating the hook installation to always set the currently configured root resolved both failures.

I reran the focused gate test file; all tests passed. I then reran the full required command, `REPOOS_CHECK_CHANGED=main repoos check`. The remote runner retried after two hosts were reported hung; the third attempt completed the build and scoped suite. Local guards, UI smoke, and rendered contrast audit also passed.

## Challenges and blockers

The main challenge is that a lock file alone does not provide lifecycle coverage. The handoff check is started by a distinct server flow, while managed self-checks and close-out checks have separate orchestration. A complete implementation must acquire and release in each owning flow, including cancellation and process restart, without creating overlapping recovery and acquisition races.

The queue uses atomic file replacement for individual writes, but that does not make a read-modify-write sequence safe across multiple server processes. Concurrent enqueues can still overwrite each other, and recovery can race with a new acquisition. A per-task cross-process mutex or another transactional queue design is needed, with stale-owner recovery and tests that exercise overlapping processes. This session did not implement that synchronization.

Source-write protection is likewise not complete for arbitrary filesystem writes. The Git wrappers and `writeWorktreeSourceFile` can reject source changes, but the latter has no broad production usage and cannot prevent an agent tool from writing directly. Wiring the refusal into the actual tool write boundary (or another enforceable worktree fence) remains necessary.

The check command automatically created WIP self-check checkpoint commits while running, as shown in its output. I did not run `git add` or `git commit` manually; the command’s built-in checkpoint behavior changed HEAD as part of the requested verification.

## Key learnings

A behavior helper is not evidence of a production fix until the real gate path calls it. Handoff’s earlier tests proved path classification but could not catch that the finalization code still used a separate task-file-only exception. The board root also needs to be an explicit part of the commit hook context whenever the command runs from a linked task worktree.

Deferred bookkeeping should preserve the on-disk authoritative state and keep durable queue records until commits succeed. Replaying a captured file snapshot is unsafe when multiple writes can target the same path during a gate. Atomic JSON replacement protects against torn files, but cross-process coordination is still needed to avoid lost updates.

Finally, the scoped check is expensive when it dispatches remote validation: this run needed host failover before completing. Focused tests helped isolate the root-resolution regression quickly, but the final required check was still necessary to confirm the changed tree and repository gates together.
